Vibresia vs Plane9: the free alternative for a Mac

By Syd Lawrence, a visual artist and developer who makes Vibresia. Facts last checked 2 November 2026; updated 2 November 2026.

Plane9 doesn't run on a Mac: its download page lists Windows only. If you're on a Mac and want what Plane9 gives Windows users, free visuals that move with the music, Vibresia is the alternative: it's free, it listens to whatever the Mac is playing, and you can write new scenes or have an AI assistant write them. On Windows, Plane9 is still the pick, with far more scenes and VR support. We make Vibresia, so check our reasons against the sources at the bottom.

Pick Vibresia if

you're on a Mac with Apple silicon and want free visuals for Spotify, Apple Music, a browser or a film, and you'd like to write new scenes as code or by describing them to an AI assistant.

Pick Plane9 if

you're on Windows and want a free 3D visualiser or screensaver with hundreds of scenes, or you want to watch in an Oculus Rift or HTC Vive. Vibresia doesn't run on Windows and has no VR mode.

Why Vibresia is the pick on a Mac

Plane9 is a free 3D music visualiser and screensaver, and it's well loved on Windows. But it is Windows only. Its download page lists Windows 7 to 10, and the latest version listed is 2.5.1.3, from 29 December 2016, so it hasn't had a new release in years either.

Vibresia is built for the Mac and is updated now: it checks for updates on launch and installs them from the menu. It listens to the Mac's system audio, so it reacts to Spotify, Apple Music, a browser tab or a film without a plug-in, and it can use the microphone instead. It analyses the music on the Mac, picks out the beat, the bass, mids and treble and the tempo, and hands all of it to the scene on screen.

It's free in the same way Plane9 is: no price, no ads. It's also open source under the MIT licence, and there's no account to make.

Scenes: hundreds to choose from, or ones you write

Plane9's strength is its library. Its download page lists over 250 scenes, which it can combine, with 39 transitions between them. Vibresia has 18 built-in scenes, so if variety out of the box is what you want, Plane9 has more.

Vibresia makes up for it by letting you make more. A scene is a single GLSL function, vec3 render(vec2 p, float t), with the music already analysed for you. The app compiles it and explains errors in plain words before it saves. If you'd rather not write code, an AI assistant can write one from a description, using the local MCP server the app ships with. A scene you like can be shared as a short link that plays in any browser, with or without the app.

Where Plane9 is the better choice

On a Windows PC, use Plane9: Vibresia is Mac only, and needs macOS 14.2 or later, Apple silicon, so it won't run on an Intel Mac either. Plane9 also works as a screensaver and in Oculus Rift and HTC Vive headsets, and Vibresia does neither.

If you're looking at other visualisers for the Mac too, the best music visualizers for Mac lists seven of them, with prices.

Questions people ask

Is there a Plane9 for Mac?

No. Plane9's download page lists Windows 7 to 10 only. On a Mac, Vibresia is a free visualiser that reacts to whatever is playing.

Is Vibresia free like Plane9?

Yes. Vibresia is free with every feature, no ads and no account, and it's open source under the MIT licence.

Can Vibresia run as a screensaver?

No. Vibresia runs as an app, in a window or full screen. Plane9 has a screensaver mode, on Windows.

Does Vibresia work on an Intel Mac?

No. It needs macOS 14.2 or later on Apple silicon.
